chunks: Well, it is as though I see a misguided man who is shouting in Syria and has put his banners in the outskirts of Kūfah.

When his mouth would be fully opened, his recalcitrance would become intense and his steps on earth would become heavy (and tyrannic) then the disorder (so created) would cut the people with its teeth and war would rage with (all) its waves, days would become severe and nights full of toil.
So when the crop grows and stands on stalks, its foam shoots forth and its lightning shines, the banners of misguiding rebellion would fire up and shoot forth like darkening night and surging sea.
This and how many other storms would rend Kūfah and gales would sweep over it, and shortly heads would clash with heads, the standing crop would be harvested and the harvest would be smashed.
ai.seo_question: What metaphors does Imam Ali use to describe the rise of Mu'awiya and the ensuing civil war in Kufah?
ai.summary: Imam Ali (peace be upon him) vividly describes the rise of Mu'awiya from Syria, whose encroachment into Kufah signals the onset of the First Fitna, a pivotal era of civil strife in Shia historiography. The passage employs potent agricultural and meteorological metaphors to depict the escalation of conflict, culminating in the clash of generations and the 'harvesting the standing crop,' a prophetic allusion to the sudden, violent death of the Imam himself amidst the turmoil.

en.sayed-ali-raza: Well, it is as though I see a misguided man [1] who is shouting in Syria (ash-Shām) and has put his banners in the outskirt of Kūfah.

When his mouth would be fully opened, his recalcitrance would become intense and his steps on earth would become heavy (and tyrannic) then the disorder (so created) would cut the people with its teeth and war would rage with (all) its waves, days would become severe and nights full of toil.
So when the crop grows and stands on stalks, its foam shoots forth and its lightning shines, the banners of misguiding rebellion would fire up and shoot forth like darkening night and surging sea.
This and how many other storms would rend Kūfah and gales would sweep over it, and shortly heads would clash with heads, the standing crop would be harvested and the harvest would be smashed.
